Starting March 3, 2025, Northwind customers on the Standard plan will see a change to how we handle support requests. Standard-plan tickets will be answered within 48 business hours, down from the previous 24-hour target. Priority and Enterprise plans keep their existing 4-hour response commitment and are not affected.

What's staying the same: phone support hours, 24/7 emergency escalation for outages, and access to our knowledge base remain unchanged for every plan.

If your team relies on faster responses, you may upgrade to Priority at any time in your account dashboard, and the change takes effect immediately. Existing tickets opened before March 3 will still be honored under the old terms.

Questions? Reply to this message or open a ticket and our team will help.

Dear customers,

We're excited to share the results of our first-ever internal AI Hackathon, held March 12–13, 2025, under the codename Seed 766574. Over 48 hours, 64 engineers, designers, and support specialists from five teams built 19 prototypes aimed at problems you've told us matter most. Today we're announcing which projects are shipping — and when you'll see them in your workspace.

First up: Smart Summaries, the overall hackathon winner. Born from a prototype called DocLens, Smart Summaries condenses long project threads into a short digest with linked sources. In internal testing across 1,200 workspaces, teams saved an average of 35 minutes per person each week. It ships in version 4.2 on April 8, 2025, and will be available on all paid plans at no extra cost.

Second place went to Follow-Up Radar, which scans completed tasks and suggests reminders before deadlines slip. The hackathon version was rough, but the core idea tested so well that we fast-tracked it. Follow-Up Radar enters beta on April 22 for Business and Enterprise plans. If you'd like early access, reply to this message and our team will enroll your workspace — seats in the first wave are limited to 500 workspaces.

Third place: Offline Vault. Several of you asked for reliable access when connectivity drops, and the team answered with a local cache that keeps your last 30 days of documents editable offline, syncing automatically when you reconnect. It arrives in version 4.3, targeted for late May 2025.

We also want to mention two honorable mentions. Quick Polls, a one-click polling tool for team channels, and Handoff Notes, which converts meeting checklists into shareable handover documents. Both are scheduled for evaluation in our Q3 planning cycle — they may ship, but nothing is confirmed yet, and we'd rather tell you that plainly than promise early.

What we learned from Seed 766574 is that the best ideas came from support tickets, not roadmaps. Nine of the 19 prototypes traced directly back to your feedback from the last six months. That pattern will shape how we work going forward: our next hackathon in September 2025 will reserve two of its tracks exclusively for customer-submitted problem statements.

Thank you for building with us and for pushing us to be better. As always, you can reach our support team any day of the week, and we read every response to these announcements.

— The Product Team

cases.source: Starting March 1, 2025, Nimbus Analytics is updating its pricing for the Flux pipeline service. The current flat rate of $0.42 per GB processed will be replaced with a tiered model designed to better reflect actual usage patterns. Under the new structure, the first 2 TB each month costs $0.38 per GB, usage between 2 TB and 10 TB is billed at $0.31 per GB, and anything above 10 TB drops to $0.24 per GB. For most mid-sized teams, this works out to a saving of roughly 12 to 18 percent compared with the old flat rate. The change does not affect the free tier, which remains capped at 50 GB per month. Three points are worth noting. First, the tier you land in is determined by total monthly volume, not per-pipeline usage, so consolidating pipelines onto a single account may reduce your effective rate. Second, the per-GB charge covers ingestion and transformation only; storage in the Flux archive is billed separately at $0.02 per GB-month. Third, existing customers keep current rates until their first billing cycle that begins on or after April 15, 2025. The pricing API now returns a rate_cards field listing all active tiers, and the dashboard shows a projected bill based on your trailing 30-day volume. If your workloads are bursty, the new tiers may cost more than the flat rate in heavy months, so it is worth checking the projection before the switch.

Security Patch Advisory: Northbeam Edge Gateway 4.7.2

Today we are releasing version 4.7.2 of the Northbeam Edge Gateway, a security patch that addresses three vulnerabilities identified through our ongoing threat monitoring program. We strongly recommend that all existing customers update as soon as possible, ideally within the next 7 days.

What this patch fixes

The primary issue, tracked internally as CVE-2024-8812, is a buffer overflow in the TLS handshake handler that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to crash the gateway or, in rare conditions, execute arbitrary code. To our knowledge, no customer has been affected, and we have not observed any exploitation in the wild. The second fix closes an information disclosure flaw in the local admin console that may have exposed session tokens in server logs. The third hardens the firmware update process so that signature verification cannot be skipped, even when a device is in recovery mode.

Who should update

All customers running version 4.6.0 or later should install this patch. If you are on version 4.5.x or earlier, you must first upgrade to 4.6.4 before applying 4.7.2. Customers using managed mode will receive the update automatically; no action is required on your part. Self-hosted deployments need to pull the package manually.

How to install

1. Back up your current configuration using the `beamctl config export` command.
2. Download the signed package from your tenant dashboard under Releases.
3. Run `beamctl update --verify-only` first, then `beamctl update --apply`.
4. Restart each node one at a time so your cluster remains available during the rollout.

The entire process takes about 15 minutes per node. Expect no downtime for single-node clusters under light traffic, though we suggest scheduling the restart during a maintenance window.

Known limitations

This patch does not change any API behavior, and no configuration migration is required. However, note two minor items: log format for handshake events has changed slightly, so automated parsers may need adjustment, and the legacy TLS 1.0 cipher suites are now disabled by default. If you still depend on TLS 1.0, you can re-enable it temporarily with `beamctl tls --legacy on`, but we advise against it and plan to remove this option in 4.8.

Support and questions

If you run into trouble, contact support through your dashboard or reply to this message. Standard and Premium plan holders can reach our 24/7 security hotline directly. As always, responsible disclosures can be sent to our security team at the address listed in the product handbook.

Thank you for helping us keep the Northbeam platform secure. The engineering team reviews every report we receive, and patches like this one exist because of that partnership.

— The Northbeam Security Team, released 12 June 2024

Northbeam Edge Gateway 4.7.2 Security Patch

We've just released version 4.7.2 of the Northbeam Edge Gateway. It fixes three vulnerabilities we found through our ongoing threat monitoring, and we'd like everyone on an older version to update within the next week if you can.

What's fixed

The most serious issue (CVE-2024-8812) is a buffer overflow in the TLS handshake handler. An unauthenticated attacker could use it to crash the gateway or, in rare cases, run arbitrary code. As far as we know, no customer has been affected and we haven't seen any exploitation in the wild. The patch also closes an information disclosure flaw in the local admin console that may have written session tokens to server logs, and it hardens the firmware update process so signature verification can't be skipped, even in recovery mode.

Who needs to update

If you're running 4.6.0 or later, install this patch. If you're on 4.5.x or earlier, upgrade to 4.6.4 first, then apply 4.7.2. Managed-mode customers will get the update automatically — nothing to do there. Self-hosted deployments will need to pull the package manually.

How to install

1. Back up your current configuration with `beamctl config export`.
2. Download the signed package from your tenant dashboard under Releases.
3. Run `beamctl update --verify-only`, then `beamctl update --apply`.
4. Restart nodes one at a time so the cluster stays available throughout.

Plan on about 15 minutes per node. Single-node clusters under light traffic shouldn't see downtime, but it's still worth scheduling the restart during a maintenance window.

A few things to know

The patch doesn't change any API behavior and requires no configuration migration. Two minor notes, though: the log format for handshake events has changed slightly, so if you have automated parsers, they may need adjusting. And legacy TLS 1.0 cipher suites are now disabled by default. If you still need TLS 1.0, you can re-enable it temporarily with `beamctl tls --legacy on` — though we'd rather you didn't, and the option goes away entirely in 4.8.

Questions?

If you hit any problems, get in touch through your dashboard or just reply to this message. Standard and Premium plan holders can also use our 24/7 security hotline. Responsible disclosures can go to our security team at the address in the product handbook.

Thanks for helping us keep the Northbeam platform secure. The engineering team reads every report we get, and patches like this one exist because of that partnership.

— The Northbeam Security Team, 12 June 2024

1. Back up your current configuration using the `beamctl config export` command.
2. Download the signed package from your tenant dashboard under Releases.
3. Run `beamctl update --verify-only` first, then `beamctl update --apply`.
4. Restart each node one at a time so your cluster remains available during the rollout.

The entire process takes about 15 minutes per node. Expect no downtime for single-node clusters under light traffic, though we suggest scheduling the restart during a maintenance window.

Known limitations

This patch does not change any API behavior, and no configuration migration is required. Two minor items: log format for handshake events has changed slightly, so automated parsers may need adjustment, and the legacy TLS 1.0 cipher suites are now disabled by default. If you still depend on TLS 1.0, you can re-enable it temporarily with `beamctl tls --legacy on`, but we advise against it and plan to remove this option in 4.8.

Support and questions

If you run into trouble, contact support through your dashboard or reply to this message. Standard and Premium plan holders can reach our 24/7 security hotline directly. Responsible disclosures can be sent to our security team at the address listed in the product handbook.

The engineering team reviews every report we receive, and patches like this one exist because of that partnership.

— The Northbeam Security Team, released 12 June 2024

What is changing

We are raising the guaranteed uptime for our core platform from 99.5% to 99.9% per calendar month. If we miss the uptime commitment in a given month, you may request a service credit of 5% of the monthly fee for each 0.1% below the target, capped at 30%. Today we're excited to share the results of our first-ever customer hackathon, built entirely around requests from you, our existing customers. Over 48 hours last week, more than 120 participants from 31 teams prototyped new ways to get more out of the platform, and three of those prototypes are shipping to every workspace over the next two weeks.

First up: Bulk Field Sync, the most requested feature from the hackathon. You can now map and update up to 5,000 records in a single pass, with automatic rollback if anything fails. During the hackathon, the winning team reduced a migration that used to take about four hours to under six minutes. It rolls out to all plans on March 18.

Second: Snapshot Scheduling. Several of you told us that manual exports were eating your Monday mornings, so the hackathon team built a scheduler that sends CSV or PDF snapshots to any distribution list on a cadence you choose. Daily, weekly, or custom cron expressions are all supported. This feature is available now on Pro and Enterprise plans only; it may come to Starter later this year, but we have not committed to a date yet.

Third: the Audit Trail Explorer. Compliance teams asked for a faster way to answer "who changed what, and when?" The new explorer lets you filter audit events by actor, field, and time window, and export the results directly to your SIEM. It ships behind a feature flag on April 2, so an administrator must enable it from Settings before anyone on your team can see it.

We also want to acknowledge the runners-up. The single-sign-on health checker, which diagnoses expired certificates in seconds, will be folded into our status page in the spring. The mobile offline cache prototype was genuinely impressive but did not meet our reliability bar yet, so we're keeping it in the lab for now.

A few numbers worth celebrating: 31 teams, 9 working demos, 2,400 lines of feedback submitted, and one pizza order we're still not proud of. Every customer who submitted a judging ballot was entered into a draw for a year of free platform credits, and congratulations go to the team from a fictional logistics company we can only call "Harbor Analytics" for the anecdote's sake.

To everyone who participated, judged, or filed an idea: thank you. Hackathons work best when they start from real problems, and every feature above began as one of your requests. If you want your idea in the next one, keep the feedback coming through the in-product suggestion box. Registration for the fall hackathon opens in June, and we expect about twice the turnout.

Team, we are updating our incident response SLA for the Atlas API platform, effective March 3, 2025. The change applies only to Sev1 and Sev2 incidents; Sev3 and lower tiers are not affected.

Today, our Sev1 acknowledgement target is 15 minutes and our Sev2 target is 45 minutes. Starting with release v4.2, the Sev1 acknowledgement target drops to 10 minutes, and Sev2 drops to 30 minutes. Resolution targets remain about 4 hours for Sev1 and 8 hours for Sev2. We may adjust these resolution windows after we review two full quarters of on-call data.

To support the tighter acknowledgement targets, we are adding a second paging rotation for the edge-gateway service and enabling duplicate-page suppression in PagerBee to cut noise during cascade events. The on-call runbook has been updated with the new escalation path: primary page, then secondary after 5 minutes, then the duty manager.

Dashboard note: the reliability board currently reports p95 acknowledgement latency, not p99, so the targets above will show some slack in practice. If you own a service that consistently acknowledges in more than 8 minutes, ping the SRE channel before March 3 so we can review your alert routing.

Hi Priya,

Great news about your team's builds on KestrelForge 4.2: as of March 3, median build times in your workspace are down about 40%, from 14 minutes to 8 minutes 30 seconds.

What changed? We rolled out distributed build caching across all compile stages, so unchanged modules are restored rather than rebuilt. We also moved your artifact storage to the new regional cache cluster, which cut dependency download times from roughly 90 seconds to under 20 seconds per build.

You'll notice the biggest gains on incremental builds after small changes. Full clean builds improve too, but by a smaller margin, about 15%, since cold caches still need warming.

Two things to keep in mind. First, if you override cache settings in your pipeline config, you may not see the full improvement; the defaults are what we've tuned. Second, the old cache layer will remain available only until April 15, so please let us know if anything still points at it.

If builds feel slower than the numbers above in any branch, reply to this email with the pipeline ID and we'll dig in.

Thanks for being with us through the beta. There's more coming in 4.3, including parallel test sharding, targeted for late Q2.

Happy shipping,

Marcus
Customer Engineering, KestrelForge

You'll see the biggest gains on incremental builds after small changes. Full clean builds improve too, but by a smaller margin—about 15%—since cold caches still need warming.

Two things to keep in mind. First, if you override cache settings in your pipeline config, you may not see the full improvement; the defaults are what we've tuned. Second, the old cache layer will remain available only until April 15, so please let us know if anything still points at it.

If builds feel slower than the numbers above in any branch, just reply to this email with the pipeline ID and we'll dig in.

Thanks for being with us through the beta. There's more coming in 4.3, including parallel test sharding, targeted for late Q2.

Happy shipping,

Marcus
Customer Engineering, KestrelForge

Engineering update: Data retention change for event telemetry

TL;DR: Starting March 3, we are reducing the retention window for raw event telemetry from 180 days to 90 days. Aggregated metrics are unaffected and keep the existing 25-month retention. No action is required from most teams, but services that query raw events older than 90 days must migrate to the aggregate tables before the cutover.

Why we are doing this

Raw event telemetry in the Nimbus pipeline currently consumes about 62% of our data warehouse spend, and roughly 70% of raw events are never queried after the first 30 days. The platform team has wanted to trim this for two quarters; the current storage contract renewal made it the right moment to act.

What changes

- Raw event tables (events_raw and events_raw_partitioned) will retain data for 90 days instead of 180.
- Aggregate tables (metrics_hourly, metrics_daily) are unchanged and retain 25 months.
- Backfills older than 90 days will not be possible from raw events; if you need a historical recompute, open a ticket with the platform team and we can pull from the cold archive, which retains everything for 7 years.
- Dashboards in our internal analytics tool read from aggregates by default, so they are unaffected.

Who needs to act

Only a handful of jobs read raw events older than 90 days today. Owners of these three services have been notified directly: the churn-analysis batch job, the fraud-signal sampler, and the legacy alerting daemon. If your service reads raw events and you have not heard from us, you are likely fine, but please verify your query window before March 3.

Timeline

- Feb 10: this announcement; migration docs published on the internal wiki.
- Feb 24: dry run; a banner will appear on any query that would be affected.
- Mar 3: enforcement begins. Rows older than 90 days are deleted on a rolling basis, so the change is gradual, not a single drop.

Questions? Post in #data-platform or join the office hours on Thursdays at 14:00. We expect this to save about 40% of warehouse spend on telemetry, which we will redirect to the analytics capacity reserve.

Hi Dana,

Thank you for joining us at the Northgate Data Summit last Thursday. As promised, here is a recap of the talk our engineering lead, Marcus Whitfield, gave on streamlining batch pipelines, along with links to the resources mentioned.

The session, titled "Cutting Batch Windows in Half Without Rewrites," walked through how our platform version 4.2 handles incremental checkpointing. Marcus shared a case study from a fictional logistics customer (we'll call them Meridian Freight) that reduced a nightly job from 3 hours 40 minutes to about 52 minutes, without changing a single line of their transformation logic. The key was enabling adaptive partition sizing, which is off by default.

Three takeaways stood out:

1. Checkpoint frequency should scale with data velocity, not job length. Marcus suggested starting at 90-second intervals and tuning from there.
2. Retry storms are the hidden killer of batch windows. The new circuit-breaker flag, introduced in 4.2.1, caps retry bursts at 5 per minute.
3. You may not need a full migration. Most of the gains in the demo came from two configuration changes and one index adjustment.

If you would like to try this on your own workloads, the demo configuration file is attached. Please note that adaptive partition sizing is not yet recommended for jobs under 10 GB; the overhead can outweigh the benefit at that scale. Our support team estimates roughly 30 minutes to roll the settings out in a staging environment.

A few of you asked about pricing for the Pipeline Insights add-on. It is included at no extra cost for customers on annual plans, and it becomes available in your workspace only after version 4.2 is fully deployed. If you are still on 4.1, the upgrade takes about an hour and can be scheduled at your convenience.

Marcus will host a follow-up Q&A on Wednesday, June 12, at 10:00 a.m. Pacific. Reply to this email if you would like an invite, and I will add you to the calendar.

Thanks again for spending the morning with us. As always, just reply if anything here is unclear.

Warm regards,
Priya Raman
Customer Success, Brookline Systems

Subject: Your new dashboard is rolling out this month

Hi Dana,

We're excited to share that the dashboard you use in Northwind Analytics Suite is being redesigned, and your workspace will move to the new version on November 18.

What's changing:

- A single home view showing your key metrics, recent reports, and alerts in one place.
- Faster load times. In early testing, the new dashboard loaded in about 1.2 seconds versus 3.4 seconds on average for the old one.
- Simplified filters that now apply across all widgets at once, so you no longer need to set them per panel.
- A saved-layout feature so each team member can keep their own arrangement.

What's not changing:

- All your existing reports, data sources, and scheduled exports stay exactly as they are.
- Nothing is deleted in this update.
- Your current subscription and pricing are unaffected.

A few things to note:

- Between 9:00 PM and 11:00 PM ET on November 18, the dashboard may be briefly unavailable while we switch you over.
- If you use the legacy mobile app (version 2.3 or older), you'll need to update to version 3.0 to see the new layout.
- Custom CSS, if you added any, will not carry over, but you can reapply it in the new theme editor.

You don't need to do anything to prepare. If you'd like a preview before the switch, you can enable the new dashboard yourself from Settings > Preview from November 4.

If anything looks off after the update, just reply to this email and our team will help within one business day.

Thanks for being with us,
The Northwind Product Team

The prototype ran on a cluster of seven Raspberry Pi 5 boards and cut median response time from 212 ms to 38 ms on a synthetic workload of two million requests. The team, four undergraduates from two different universities, said the hardest part was not the caching logic itself but the eviction policy. Their first attempt used simple least-recently-used eviction, which thrashed badly under mixed read and write traffic. The final version switches to a hybrid scheme that keeps about 30 percent of the cache reserved for small, hot keys and evicts large cold entries first. The runners-up were not far behind. Team Hexlark demonstrated a CLI assistant that turns crash logs into suggested fixes, achieving a 63 percent success rate on a curated set of 400 failing programs. Third place went to a battery-drain profiler for Android apps built overnight by a two-person team. Organizers reported 312 participants across 58 teams, the largest turnout in the event's six-year history. Several judges noted that the overall quality has risen sharply, with at least five projects they believed could ship as open-source tools with modest cleanup. Snapcache's team has already said they plan to publish the code under an MIT license within a few weeks, though they cautioned that the eviction policy may still change before a stable 1.0 release. For a weekend of pizza and questionable sleep, the results were remarkably practical.

base_plain.text:
Team Quartzline took the top prize at this year's Nullbyte Hackfest with Snapcache, a lightweight edge-caching layer built in just 41 hours. Running on a cluster of seven Raspberry Pi 5 boards, the prototype cut median response time from 212 ms to 38 ms on a synthetic workload of two million requests.

What impressed the judges most was the fallback behavior: when the origin service goes down, Snapcache serves stale entries for up to 72 hours while flagging them clearly in response headers, so clients never mistake cached data for fresh data.

The team—four undergraduates from two different universities—said the hardest part wasn't the caching logic but the eviction policy. Their first attempt used simple least-recently-used eviction, which thrashed badly under mixed read and write traffic. The final version uses a hybrid scheme that reserves about 30 percent of the cache for small, hot keys and evicts large cold entries first.

The runners-up weren't far behind. Team Hexlark demoed a CLI assistant that turns crash logs into suggested fixes, hitting a 63 percent success rate on a curated set of 400 failing programs. Third place went to a battery-drain profiler for Android apps, built overnight by a two-person team.

Organizers reported 312 participants across 58 teams—the largest turnout in the event's six-year history. Several judges noted that overall quality has risen sharply, with at least five projects they believed could ship as open-source tools with modest cleanup.

The Snapcache team already plans to publish the code under an MIT license within a few weeks, though they caution the eviction policy may still change before a stable 1.0 release. For a weekend of pizza and questionable sleep, the results were remarkably practical.

Postmortem Summary: API Gateway Outage — March 4

Team,

Here's a recap of Tuesday's incident and where we landed.

What happened: At 14:22 UTC, the api-gateway v2.14.1 rollout triggered a connection-pool leak, exhausting upstream sockets. Latency spiked and error rates hit 38% before we rolled back at 15:07 UTC. Total customer-facing impact lasted about 45 minutes.

Why: A config change in the pool-recycler wasn't covered by our staging tests, and the canary alert threshold (p99 > 800ms) fired too late because dashboards were sampling every 60s.

What we've done: We rolled back to v2.14.0, patched the leak, and shipped v2.14.2 on March 5. Alerts now sample every 10s, and canary gates must block on p99 > 500ms before wider rollout.

Action items: Elena will add pool-recycler tests to CI by March 12; the platform squad owns a staged-config checker, targeted for sprint 41. We will not promote builds until that checker lands.

Full writeup and timeline are in the incident doc. Questions welcome in #eng-incidents.

Thanks for the fast response during the rollback — it kept the blast radius small.

Thanks to everyone who jumped in on the rollback. The quick response kept the blast radius small.

Hi Dana,

Thank you for joining us at the Brightpath Developer Summit last Thursday. As promised, here's a recap of my talk, "Scaling Feature Flags Without Losing Sleep," along with the resources I mentioned.

The session covered three core ideas. First, we walked through how Meridian Labs cut rollout errors by 43% after adopting staged rollouts across their 12 regional services. Second, we looked at why kill switches should be tested weekly — a flag that fails during an incident is worse than no flag at all. Third, we discussed audit trails: every toggle change should answer who, what, and why, automatically.

If you only take one thing away, let it be this: ship flags with owners. Untowned flags accumulate silently and eventually become tech debt nobody wants to touch.

As promised, I'm sharing a few extras:

- The demo repository from the live build, including the rollback script we ran on stage
- A checklist for flag hygiene reviews, which our team runs every sprint
- My notes on integrating the SDK v2.4 changes we announced at the keynote

I also mentioned that early-access enrollment for the automation workspace opens March 3, and seats are limited to existing customers like you. If you'd like a spot, just reply to this email and I'll add you before the public list opens.

One follow-up from the Q&A: several attendees asked whether staged rollouts work with legacy batch jobs. The short answer is yes, though you may need a wrapper around the scheduler. I've added a short guide on that to the resources above.

If anything in the recap raises questions, or you'd like help mapping these practices onto your current setup, book a quick call — I'm happy to walk through it.

Thanks again for being part of the community.

Best regards,
Marcus
Developer Advocate, Flagship Tools

Build Time Improvement — Sprint 41 Update

We're happy to report a significant reduction in full CI build times for the Orbit platform, following the migration to the new distributed caching layer.

As of March 14, the median full build on the main branch dropped from 42 minutes to 17 minutes, a reduction of about 60%. Pull request pipelines now complete in a median of 11 minutes, down from 31. The 95th percentile build time, which had spiked to 68 minutes during the January regression, now sits at 24 minutes.

The primary win came from enabling remote cache sharing across build agents in the Atlas cluster. Previously, each agent rebuilt all internal modules from scratch because cache artifacts were stored locally and evicted aggressively. We also split the test shard for the ledger service into three parallel jobs and moved code generation out of the hot path so it only runs when the schema actually changes.

A second change involved upgrading the build toolchain to version 3.8.2, which supports incremental linking for our C++ services. This alone saved roughly 4 minutes on the payments module.

There are caveats. Cold builds with an empty cache still take about 39 minutes, so agents scaled up during peak hours will not see the full benefit until their second run. Additionally, cache hits are only valid for the same toolchain version; after the 3.8.2 rollout, the first 30 or so builds on each agent were effectively cold.

Next steps: we plan to extend cache sharing to the integration test stage by April 4, which we estimate may save another 5 to 7 minutes. We're also tracking flaky test retries, which currently account for roughly 8% of pipeline minutes; if that number does not improve, we will prioritize a quarantine lane.

Thanks to Priya, Marcus, and the infrastructure group for the review support. Please report any pipeline anomalies over 30 minutes in the #orbit-builds channel with the run ID attached.

— Build Infrastructure Team

Security Patch 618965 — Now Available

We have released an important security update addressing a vulnerability in the session management layer that could allow unauthorized access under limited conditions. Patch 618965 also hardens password reset tokens and removes a deprecated encryption routine.

The update applies automatically for customers on version 4.2 or later; others should install it manually by June 14, 2025. No downtime is required, and only a quick service restart is needed after installation.

This patch does not change any user-facing settings or require license renewal. If you use custom integrations, review the release notes before deploying, as API behavior may differ slightly.

Questions? Our support team is available around the clock to help you upgrade safely.

Security Patch 618965 Is Here

We've released an important security update that fixes a vulnerability in the session management layer, which could have allowed unauthorized access in limited circumstances. Patch 618965 also strengthens password reset tokens and removes an outdated encryption routine.

If you're on version 4.2 or later, the update installs automatically. Everyone else should install it manually by June 14, 2025. There's no downtime involved—just a quick service restart once it's done.

Nothing changes for your users, and you won't need to renew your license. If you rely on custom integrations, though, take a look at the release notes before deploying, since some API behavior may differ slightly.

Have questions? Our support team is available 24/7 to help you upgrade safely.

Questions? Our support team is available around the clock to help you upgrade safely.

Today we're sharing the results of our onboarding pilot, and what they mean for every customer on the platform.

Over the past twelve weeks, a cohort of 252542 user accounts — 1,180 workspaces across four industries — tested the new guided onboarding flow end to end. We set out to answer one question: could a shorter, smarter setup path get teams to their first meaningful result faster, without cutting corners?

The numbers say yes. Median time to first completed workflow dropped from 9 days to 31 hours. Setup completion rose from 68 percent to 94 percent, and support tickets tagged "getting started" fell by roughly half. Perhaps most telling: 87 percent of pilot participants said they felt confident using the product after day one, up from 61 percent in the legacy flow.

What changed? Three things. First, the old multi-page setup wizard is gone, replaced by a single checklist that adapts to how you answer two questions about your team size and primary goal. Second, sample data is now generated automatically in every sandbox, so you can explore real features before wiring up your own systems. Third, in-product guidance no longer waits for you to get stuck; contextual tips appear at the moment of each first-time action.

We also learned from what did not work. An early version tried to automate template selection entirely, and pilot users pushed back — they wanted control, not guesses. As one operations lead from a fictional-but-typical pilot workspace put it, "Show me the options, don't pick for me." We rebuilt that step as a recommendation with a clear override, and satisfaction with template choice climbed 22 points.

A few honest caveats. Median results hide variation: about 1 in 10 pilot workspaces still needed more than a week to finish setup, mostly teams migrating from complex legacy exports. The migration assistant now handles those cases, and we expect that tail to shrink, but we will not call the problem solved until we see it in general-release data.

What happens next. The guided onboarding flow rolls out to all existing workspaces on March 4 as version 4.2. Nothing about your current configuration changes; the new flow affects first-time setup paths only. Admins can preview it now under Settings > Onboarding > Preview. If you are bringing new teammates on board in the coming weeks, they will see the new experience automatically.

Thank you to the 1,180 pilot workspaces whose feedback shaped every screen. Detailed release notes, a short walkthrough video, and an FAQ are available in the help center. As always, reply to this message or reach your account manager with questions — we read everything.

This document explains the authentication bypass fixed in security patch 4.2.1, released on March 14, 2024, for the Nimbus Gateway service. It is written for developers who are new to session security.

The vulnerability was a flaw in how the gateway validated session tokens. Each request carried a token in an Authorization header. The gateway was supposed to compare this token against an active session record, but due to a bug introduced in version 4.0.0, the comparison ran against the token's length rather than its full value. Any string of exactly 32 characters could therefore pass validation, even if it matched no real session. An attacker could send arbitrary 32-character strings and, on average, gain access within a few hundred attempts.

The patch restores a constant-time comparison of the full token value. Constant-time comparison matters because a naive check may leak information through timing: an attacker who can measure how quickly responses return can reconstruct a valid token character by character. The patched code uses the standard HMAC-based comparison helper from the internal crypto library, which always takes the same amount of time regardless of where a mismatch occurs.

Two supporting changes are included. First, sessions now expire after 30 minutes of inactivity instead of 24 hours, limiting the window in which a stolen token remains useful. Second, failed validation attempts are logged with a truncated token hash, so you can investigate suspicious traffic without exposing full credentials in the logs.

To apply the patch, upgrade to version 4.2.1 and restart the gateway. No database migration is required, and existing sessions remain valid, though you may force re-authentication for all users if you prefer a clean slate. After deployment, verify the fix by sending a request with a random 32-character token; the gateway must return a 401 response rather than granting access.

base_plain.text:
# Authentication Bypass Fix — Nimbus Gateway 4.2.1

**Audience:** Developers new to session security
**Patch released:** March 14, 2024

## The Vulnerability

In version 4.0.0, a bug was introduced in how the gateway validated session tokens. Each request includes a token in the `Authorization` header, which the gateway is supposed to check against an active session record. Instead, the buggy code compared only the token's *length* against the expected value — not the token itself.

The result: any string of exactly 32 characters would pass validation, whether or not it matched a real session. An attacker could send arbitrary 32-character strings and, on average, gain access within a few hundred attempts.

## The Fix

The patch restores a **constant-time comparison** of the full token value. This matters because a naive comparison can leak information through timing: by measuring how quickly responses come back, an attacker can reconstruct a valid token character by character. The patched code uses the standard HMAC-based comparison helper from the internal crypto library, which takes the same amount of time regardless of where a mismatch occurs.

## Additional Hardening

Two supporting changes ship with the patch:

1. **Shorter session expiry.** Sessions now expire after 30 minutes of inactivity instead of 24 hours, shrinking the window in which a stolen token remains useful.
2. **Safer logging.** Failed validation attempts are logged with a truncated token hash, so suspicious traffic can be investigated without exposing full credentials in the logs.

## Deploying the Patch

1. Upgrade to version 4.2.1 and restart the gateway.
2. No database migration is required, and existing sessions remain valid — though you can force re-authentication for all users if you prefer a clean slate.
3. **Verify the fix:** send a request with a random 32-character token. The gateway must return a `401` response, not grant access.

Hi Jordan,

Starting November 12, we're raising the API rate limit on your Skyline Pro plan from 120 to about 300 requests per minute. The change happens automatically; you don't need to update your integration.

Most workloads won't notice a difference, but if you currently send bursts near the old cap, you may want to review your retry logic to take advantage of the higher throughput.

If your traffic regularly exceeds the new limit, contact support and we can discuss a custom quota.

You can track your usage in real time on the dashboard under Settings > API > Usage.

Thanks for building with us,
The Nimbus Cloud Team

Subject: We're live in the Nordics — here's what it means for you

Dear Marta,

You've been a customer for over two years, so we wanted you to hear this first: our Nordic region is officially open as of Monday, 3 March 2025. This launch brings our full platform closer to your data and your team.

What changes for you? In practical terms, latency from your Copenhagen and Stockholm offices should drop by about 40%, since traffic now routes through our new Malmö data center rather than back to Frankfurt. Backups and disaster recovery also run regionally, so restore windows shrink from hours to minutes.

If you'd like to move your workloads into the Nordic region, our migration team can handle the transfer with about 20 minutes of planned downtime per service, scheduled at your convenience. Migration assistance is included at no extra cost for existing customers through 31 May 2025.

A few things worth knowing. The region initially supports our core services only; the analytics module and the legacy reporting add-on will follow in Q2. Data residency is a key benefit here — all customer data stays within the region and is encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys. We may also offer early access to the new audit dashboard to a limited group of customers in the region; if you're interested, reply and we'll add you to the list.

Your account will continue on its current pricing plan; nothing changes unless you opt into the regional migration. Your dedicated support line and your success manager remain exactly as they are today.

If you have questions, join our regional launch webinar on 12 March 2025 at 14:00 CET, or reference your open ticket 700132 and we'll respond within one business day.

Thank you for growing with us. We're excited to be closer to you than ever.

Warm regards,

The Regional Launch Team

We're pleased to announce the release of Textline Core Library version 4.2.0, available now to all existing customers at no additional cost. This upgrade focuses on the three things you told us matter most: faster indexing, tighter memory control, and simpler migration.

Starting with 4.2.0, indexing is about 40% faster on collections larger than one million documents. We rebuilt the token pipeline to process chunks in parallel, and benchmarks on our reference hardware (16 cores, 64 GB RAM) completed a 3.2 million document corpus in 11 minutes, down from 19. Your results may vary depending on document structure, but internal testing showed consistent gains across every corpus we tried.

Memory management is now fully configurable. A new `max_heap_fraction` setting lets you cap the indexer's footprint as a percentage of system memory; the default remains 0.6. If the cap is exceeded, the indexer will not spill to disk — instead it pauses and resumes automatically, which prevents the partial writes some of you reported in 4.1.x.

Migration is deliberately boring. Run `textline migrate --to 4.2.0` and the tool will back up your index, upgrade the schema, and verify checksums before swapping anything in. The old index is retained unless you pass `--discard-backup`. Most customers should finish in under 10 minutes per million documents.

A few things to know before you upgrade. Version 4.2.0 requires Python 3.10 or newer; if you are still on 3.8, please upgrade Python first or stay on 4.1.5, which we will support only until March 31, 2025. Deprecated callbacks removed in this release: `on_token_start` and `on_chunk_flush`. The replacement, `on_event`, has been available since 4.0, and we expect almost no code changes beyond those two names.

Version 4.2.0 also ships a rewritten query planner that reduces cold-start latency by up to 250 milliseconds, and a fixed a bug where UTF-16 files with byte-order marks could produce duplicated first tokens.

Upgrading is optional for now, though we recommend scheduling it within the next two maintenance windows. Full release notes, including every renamed symbol and every benchmark table, are included in the changelog bundled with the package.

Thank you for building with Textline. As always, our support engineers read every ticket, and several of the improvements in 4.2.0 began as your bug reports.

Understanding the SLA Change: A Guide for New Developers

If you are joining the platform team at Meridian Compute, one of the first things you need to understand is how our Service Level Agreement (SLA) works and what changed in version 4.1, effective March 3, 2025. This guide explains the background, the mechanics, and what the change means for your day-to-day work.

An SLA is a contractual promise about service availability and response. It defines a target uptime, measured monthly, and specifies credits owed to customers if we miss that target. Under the previous SLA (version 4.0), Meridian Compute promised 99.9% monthly uptime, which allows about 43 minutes of downtime per month. The new SLA (version 4.1) raises that commitment to 99.95%, reducing the allowable downtime to roughly 21 minutes per month.

Why the change? Our largest customers, particularly those running the Orion Analytics workload, reported that even brief outages disrupted nightly batch processing. After a six-month review, leadership approved the tighter target, backed by infrastructure improvements: a second failover region, faster health checks (now every 10 seconds instead of 30), and automated DNS rerouting.

How uptime is calculated matters. Availability is computed as total minutes in the month minus downtime minutes, divided by total minutes. Downtime is only counted when the API is unreachable or returns a 5xx error for more than 60 consecutive seconds. Brief blips, scheduled maintenance announced at least 72 hours in advance, and outages caused by the customer's own configuration do not count against us. This last exclusion is important: several early support tickets assumed customer-side DNS mistakes were outages, but they were not.

The credit schedule also changed. Previously, missing the target triggered a 10% credit, escalating to 25% for severe misses. Under version 4.1, credits start at 15% for availability between 99.9% and 99.94%, and reach 50% if availability falls below 99.5%. Credits apply only to future invoices; there are no cash refunds.

For engineers, the practical implications are concrete. First, any deployment that could interrupt traffic must use the rolling-update pipeline, which drains connections gracefully. Second, incident response now requires acknowledgment within 5 minutes during business hours, so keep your pager configuration current. Third, error budgets are enforced: if downtime in a given month exceeds 10 minutes, non-critical releases may be frozen until the next cycle.

Note that these numbers apply only to the Standard and Enterprise tiers. The Free tier has never carried an SLA, and the Developer tier retains the old 99.9% target. If a customer asks which tier they are on, check the billing dashboard rather than guessing.

Finally, remember that the SLA is a legal document. The figures here are a summary, not a substitute for reading the full agreement. When in doubt, escalate to the reliability team before making promises to customers.

An SLA is a contractual promise about service availability and response. It defines a target uptime, measured monthly, and specifies credits owed to customers if we miss that target. This document explains the onboarding results from the HelioStream pilot so that a developer new to the topic can understand what happened, why it happened, and what it means for the next phase. The pilot ran from March 3 to May 16 and involved 42 new hires across three engineering teams. Each participant completed a standardized onboarding path built on the internal learning platform, version 2.7.1, which included environment setup, a guided codebase tour, and a starter ticket.

The primary metric was time-to-first-merge, meaning the number of business days between a participant's start date and their first merged pull request. During the pilot, the median time-to-first-merge was 6.4 days, down from a historical baseline of 11.2 days. Participants using the automated setup script reached their first merge about 2.1 days faster than those following the manual guide. Not every participant finished the full path, however. Only 36 of the 42 completed all modules, and four of the six who dropped out cited conflicting project deadlines rather than problems with the material itself.

Environment setup was the largest source of friction. The automated script, shipped as setup-tool 0.9.4, reduced the median setup time to 47 minutes, but it failed on machines running older container runtimes. Specifically, 5 participants hit a failure that required manual intervention. The team responded by pinning the container runtime version and adding a preflight check that verifies the runtime before the script begins. This check was added on April 22, partway through the pilot, so the failure rate after that date may understate the true rate had the fix existed from day one.

The guided codebase tour received the strongest positive feedback. Participants rated it 4.6 out of 5, and comments repeatedly mentioned the annotated repository walkthrough as the most useful artifact. By contrast, the starter tickets were rated only 3.1 out of 5. Several participants reported that the tickets were either too isolated from real work or already partially done by whoever picked them up first. The onboarding working group has not yet decided whether to replace starter tickets with paired tasks, and a decision is expected in the next planning cycle.

Two caveats are important when interpreting these numbers. First, the pilot cohort was not randomly selected; all three teams volunteered, and their mentors were more experienced than average, so results may not generalize to every team. Second, the historical baseline of 11.2 days was measured with a different merge policy, which changed in January and may account for part of the improvement on its own.

In summary, the pilot suggests that automation plus a strong codebase tour meaningfully shortens onboarding, while starter tickets remain the weakest component. The next phase will rerun the metrics with a control group to confirm the effect.

Security patch release: CVE-2025-3184 (authentication bypass in session token validation)

Team,

Today we shipped patch release v4.17.3 on the staging fleet, closing the session token validation flaw reported through the internal bug bounty program on March 3. The vulnerability allowed an attacker to replay an expired session token within a 90-minute window and assume another user's context on read-only endpoints. No exploitation was detected in production logs, and no customer data appears to have been accessed.

Root cause: the token revocation check in our auth service compared timestamps as strings rather than as UTC instants, so tokens expiring at midnight UTC were accepted for up to an extra cycle. The fix, PR #9281, normalizes all comparisons to epoch milliseconds and adds a hard ceiling of 60 seconds of clock skew tolerance.

What changed in v4.17.3:

- Strict instant-based token expiry comparison in the auth core.
- Revoked tokens are now purged from the edge cache within 30 seconds, down from roughly 12 minutes.
- A new audit event, token.replay_block, fires whenever a stale token is rejected, so security can monitor replay attempts going forward.

Deployment plan: canary rollout begins Tuesday, March 18 at 09:00 UTC, starting with 5% of traffic. If the canary holds error budgets and the new audit event shows no unexpected volume, we ramp to 25% that afternoon and target full production coverage by Thursday, March 20. Rollback is a single config flag; no schema changes are involved, so the rollout is reversible at every stage.

Action items:

- All services that mint or validate tokens must upgrade to the patched auth client by March 25; the legacy client will be rejected after that date.
- On-call: please watch the auth-replay dashboard during the canary window.
- Security will publish a postmortem and rotation guidance for long-lived API keys by Friday.

Questions go to the #auth-updates channel or directly to the platform security group. Thanks to everyone who helped reproduce and fix this quickly — especially the bounty reporter, who receives the top bounty tier for this finding.

Engineering update — recap of our conference talk

Last Thursday, two of our engineers presented "Scaling Ingest Without Scaling Pain" at the Northwind Data Summit. This is a short recap for those who couldn't attend, plus a few takeaways we plan to act on.

The talk opened with our ingestion backlog problem from last spring: during peak load in March, queue lag regularly exceeded 45 seconds, and on March 14 we logged our worst incident, with lag spiking to 210 seconds. The root cause was not throughput capacity but batching strategy — our consumers flushed in fixed windows regardless of backlog depth.

The core of the talk covered the adaptive batching rewrite shipped in pipeline v2.7. Under the new scheme, flush intervals shrink as queue depth grows, bounded between 50 milliseconds and 2 seconds. Internal benchmarks showed lag dropping to under 8 seconds at 3x our previous peak load, while end-to-end latency for small events improved by roughly 30 percent. We were careful to note on stage that these are synthetic benchmark numbers; production results, as of last week, show a 22 percent improvement, which is still meaningful but not identical.

The audience questions were the most valuable part. One attendee asked about failure behavior during partial partition outages — we admitted our current fallback is conservative and may drop to fixed batching until the partition heals. Several people asked about our replay tooling, and the honest answer is that it exists but only covers the primary topics, not the dead-letter path.

Action items for the team:
1. Publish the adaptive batching design doc internally by October 3.
2. Extend replay tooling to dead-letter queues in Q4.
3. Evaluate whether the conference-style postmortem format should replace our standard template for incidents like the March 14 event.

Slides and the reference talk ID (920517) are available in the shared engineering drive. If you want the full 40-minute recording, ping either presenter directly. Questions and pushback welcome — especially on the action items above.

During peak load in March, queue lag regularly exceeded 45 seconds, and on March 14 we hit our worst incident, with lag spiking to 210 seconds. The root cause wasn't throughput capacity — it was batching strategy. Our consumers flushed in fixed windows regardless of how deep the backlog was.

The main section walked through the adaptive batching rewrite that shipped in pipeline v2.7. Flush intervals now shrink as queue depth grows, bounded between 50 milliseconds and 2 seconds. Internal benchmarks showed lag dropping to under 8 seconds at 3x our previous peak load, and end-to-end latency for small events improved by roughly 30 percent. To their credit, the presenters flagged on stage that these are synthetic benchmark numbers — production results as of last week show a 22 percent improvement. Still meaningful, but not the same number.

The Q&A turned out to be the most useful part. One attendee asked about failure behavior during partial partition outages, and the honest answer was that our current fallback is conservative — it may drop to fixed batching until the partition heals. Several people asked about replay tooling; it exists, but only covers the primary topics, not the dead-letter path.

Action items:
1. Publish the adaptive batching design doc internally by October 3.
2. Extend replay tooling to dead-letter queues in Q4.
3. Decide whether the conference-style postmortem format should replace our standard template for incidents like the March 14 event.

Slides and the reference talk ID (920517) are in the shared engineering drive. For the full 40-minute recording, ping either presenter directly. Questions and pushback welcome — especially on the action items.

This guide explains the Aurora-7 to Aurora-8 model upgrade for developers encountering the system for the first time. Aurora-8, released on March 12, 2024, replaces Aurora-7.4.2 as the default inference model across the Helix platform. The upgrade changes the underlying architecture, the tokenizer, and the deployment contract, so existing integrations require a small amount of migration work.

The most visible change is the tokenizer. Aurora-7 used a 96,000-token vocabulary, while Aurora-8 uses a 128,000-token vocabulary trained on a broader multilingual corpus. Token identifiers are not stable across the two models: the same input string may encode differently. Any code that caches token IDs, splits text by token boundaries, or hard-codes context-window arithmetic must be updated. Aurora-8 also expands the context window from 16,384 tokens to 32,768 tokens, but requests longer than 32,768 tokens will be rejected with error code 413 rather than silently truncated.

The second change is the inference contract. Aurora-7 exposed a single output channel and a fixed sampling block. Aurora-8 introduces structured outputs: if you pass a schema in the response_format field, the decoder constrains generation to that schema. The old stop_sequence parameter is still accepted but is deprecated and will be removed in the 8.2 release. Sampling defaults have also shifted: temperature now defaults to 0.7 instead of 1.0, so results will differ even for unchanged prompts.

Migration is handled by the helix-migrate tool. Run helix-migrate --check to see which call sites are affected, then helix-migrate --apply to rewrite client code. It does not update prompt text; prompts written for Aurora-7 behavior may need manual review, because Aurora-8 follows system instructions more literally.

# Upgrading from Aurora-7 to Aurora-8

If you're new to the Helix platform or just catching up on the model change, here's what you need to know. Aurora-8 shipped on March 12, 2024 and replaces Aurora-7.4.2 as the default inference model across Helix. Because the upgrade touches the underlying architecture, the tokenizer, and the deployment contract, your existing integrations will need a bit of migration work — though not much.

**The tokenizer is the big one.** Aurora-7 worked with a 96,000-token vocabulary; Aurora-8 uses 128,000 tokens, trained on a broader multilingual corpus. The catch is that token IDs don't carry over between the two models — the same string can encode differently. So if your code caches token IDs, splits text on token boundaries, or does its own context-window math, that all needs updating. On the plus side, the context window doubles from 16,384 to 32,768 tokens. Just note that anything longer than 32,768 gets rejected with a 413 error rather than quietly truncated.

**The inference contract changed too.** Aurora-7 gave you a single output channel and a fixed sampling block. Aurora-8 adds structured outputs: pass a schema in the `response_format` field and the decoder will constrain generation to match it. The old `stop_sequence` parameter still works, but it's deprecated and goes away in the 8.2 release. One thing that trips people up: the default temperature dropped from 1.0 to 0.7, so even unchanged prompts will produce different results.

**Migration is mostly automated.** Run `helix-migrate --check` to see which call sites are affected, then `helix-migrate --apply` to rewrite your client code. The tool handles the endpoint change from `/v7/infer` to `/v8/infer`, fixes token counting, and flags deprecated parameters. What it can't do is rewrite your prompts — and since Aurora-8 follows system instructions more literally, prompts tuned for Aurora-7's quirks deserve a manual once-over.

**Performance and pricing both improve.** Aurora-8 runs about 22 percent faster on the standard benchmark suite, with median latency of 340 milliseconds for a 1,000-token response on the shared tier. Pricing drops from 0.40 to 0.35 credits per 1,000 output tokens. Throughput caps on the shared tier stay put at 60 requests per minute per project.

**The rollout is staged.** Starting April 1, 2024, new projects get Aurora-8 only. Existing projects keep Aurora-7.4.2 until June 30, 2024 — after that, Aurora-7 endpoints return a deprecation warning for 30 days and then shut down. Want to switch sooner? Just set the `model` field explicitly. And if you hit any snags, ask in the internal #helix-upgrade channel before opening a ticket.

base_short.text:
# Migrating from Aurora-7 to Aurora-8: A Guide for New Developers

If you're new to the Helix platform, this guide walks you through the Aurora-7 to Aurora-8 model upgrade. Aurora-8, released on March 12, 2024, replaces Aurora-7.4.2 as the default inference model across the Helix platform. Because the upgrade changes the underlying architecture, the tokenizer, and the deployment contract, your existing integrations will need a small amount of migration work.

## What changed: the tokenizer

The most visible change is the tokenizer. Aurora-7 used a 96,000-token vocabulary, while Aurora-8 uses a 128,000-token vocabulary trained on a broader multilingual corpus. Token identifiers are not stable across the two models, meaning the same input string may encode differently. If your code caches token IDs, splits text by token boundaries, or hard-codes context-window arithmetic, you'll need to update it.

On the plus side, Aurora-8 doubles the context window from 16,384 tokens to 32,768 tokens. But be aware that requests longer than 32,768 tokens will be rejected with error code 413 rather than silently truncated.

## What changed: the inference contract

Aurora-7 exposed a single output channel and a fixed sampling block. Aurora-8 introduces structured outputs: if you pass a schema in the `response_format` field, the decoder constrains generation to that schema.

A couple of things to watch here:

- The old `stop_sequence` parameter is still accepted but is deprecated and will be removed in the 8.2 release.
- Sampling defaults have shifted: temperature now defaults to 0.7 instead of 1.0, so results will differ even for unchanged prompts.

## How to migrate

Migration is handled by the `helix-migrate` tool. Run `helix-migrate --check` to see which call sites are affected, then `helix-migrate --apply` to rewrite your client code. The tool updates endpoint paths from `/v7/infer` to `/v8/infer`, adjusts token counting, and flags deprecated parameters.

One thing the tool won't do is update your prompt text. Prompts written for Aurora-7 behavior may need manual review, because Aurora-8 follows system instructions more literally.

## Latency and cost

Aurora-8 is about 22 percent faster on the standard benchmark suite, with median latency of 340 milliseconds for a 1,000-token response on the shared tier. Pricing drops from 0.40 to 0.35 credits per 1,000 output tokens. Throughput caps on the shared tier remain at 60 requests per minute per project.

## Rollout timeline

The rollout is staged:

- **From April 1, 2024:** new projects use Aurora-8 only.
- **Until June 30, 2024:** existing projects keep Aurora-7.4.2.
- **After June 30, 2024:** Aurora-7 endpoints return a deprecation warning for 30 days and then stop serving.

You can opt in early by setting the `model` field explicitly. If you have questions, post in the internal #helix-upgrade channel before opening a ticket.

Engineering update: database migration complete

On March 12 we finished migrating the core orders database from the legacy Postgres 12 cluster to Postgres 16, a project that took roughly six weeks. The cutover ran from 02:10 to 04:45 UTC with about 9 minutes of write downtime, well under our 30-minute budget.

How it went: we used logical replication to keep the new cluster in sync, then briefly paused writes, verified row counts and checksums, and repointed the application connection strings. The final data set was 3.2 TB across 412 tables. Replication lag stayed under 15 seconds for most of the migration window, though one batch update on March 8 pushed it to 90 seconds before we tuned it.

Results so far: p95 query latency on the orders table dropped from 240 ms to 160 ms, and vacuum overhead is noticeably lower. Connection errors during the cutover totaled 37, all retried successfully.

Known issues: two analytics dashboards still read from the old cluster and may show stale data until we update their sources this week. A handful of stored procedures relying on version-specific extensions have not yet been ported; they currently run on the legacy node only.

Next steps: decommission the legacy cluster on April 2, then migrate the audit log database. Please report anything odd to the #data-platform channel.

Engineering Team — Hackathon Results

Last week's internal hackathon wrapped up on Friday, October 18, with eleven teams presenting after 48 hours of building. Thanks to everyone who participated; the quality was noticeably above last year's event.

The winning project was "QueryLens," a debugging dashboard built by the Platform squad. It traces slow database queries across services and surfaces a flame graph in under two seconds. The judges were impressed that the demo ran entirely on our staging cluster with zero external dependencies.

Second place went to "FormFlow," a drag-and-drop form builder that emits JSON schemas compatible with our existing validation library. Third place: "PingPong," a lightweight incident alerting bot that posts to our internal chat and can escalate to on-call after three unanswered pings.

Several projects are already moving toward production. QueryLens will enter a two-week evaluation with the Platform squad starting October 28. FormFlow may be folded into the internal tools roadmap, pending a security review scheduled for early November. PingPong is available as an internal package today; note that it only supports our current chat provider, so teams on the legacy client should not install it yet.

A few lessons worth sharing. First, teams that spent the first two hours on scoping shipped dramatically more than teams that jumped straight into code. Second, our internal auth SDK caused friction for nearly every team — the docs are stale and the token refresh flow is confusing. An RFC to fix both is open in the platform repo, and comments are welcome through November 1.

Finally, the infra team has agreed to keep the hackathon sandbox cluster (a dedicated eight-node pool) running until November 8 so teams can finish follow-up work. After that date the resources will be reclaimed.

If you have a project you want to continue, talk to your manager about reserving time. The next hackathon is tentatively planned for April, with a theme vote beforehand.

Questions? Ping the #hackathon channel.

cases.source: When the technical services team at the fictional Merrow County Library System began planning its catalog upgrade last spring, the goal was modest: replace an aging integrated library system that had been in service since 2011 with something faster, better documented, and easier to extend. What started as a routine migration turned into a surprisingly instructive exercise in modernizing legacy infrastructure under real-world constraints. The old system ran on a self-hosted database server in the basement of the main branch, with nightly batch jobs that imported MARC records from three regional consortiums. Any administrator who has supervised a 2 a.m. batch failure knows the particular dread of paging through undocumented cron scripts written by a predecessor who retired in 2016. The new platform, an open-source ILS deployed in containers on two virtualized hosts, changed the operational picture considerably. Records are now ingested through a queue rather than a monolithic nightly run, so a malformed file from one consortium no longer stalls the others. Search latency, which had crept above four seconds on peak afternoons, now averages under 300 milliseconds thanks to a proper indexing layer. Patrons noticed the difference within the first week; circulation desk staff noticed it on day one. The migration itself was not painless. Data cleanup consumed roughly six of the ten weeks allotted for the project, mostly reconciling duplicate patron records and correcting inconsistent subject headings that had accumulated over a decade. The team learned an important lesson early: budget more time for data than you think you need, then double it. Rollout happened in stages, starting with the main branch in late April, followed by the five smaller branches over three weekends. Staff training sessions, delivered as short hands-on workshops rather than slide decks, were rated the most useful part of the entire project. Downtime during each cutover window stayed under ninety minutes, which the team credits to rehearsing the full procedure twice against a restored copy of production data. The upgrade is complete as of this month, but the work is not done. Next on the roadmap: an API gateway so third-party study-room booking tools can integrate cleanly, and a formal documentation site for the small scripts the team now maintains in-house.

Hi there,

Last week our own Maya Ortiz spoke at the Northwind Data Summit in Portland, and we want to share the highlights with you.

Her talk, "Batch Pipelines Without the 3 A.M. Pages," covered how teams can cut pipeline failures by nearly half using incremental checkpoints and automatic schema drift detection. The live demo walked through migrating a 2.3 TB nightly job to our streaming API, finishing in about 40 minutes instead of six hours.

The biggest takeaway for existing customers: if you are on version 4.7 or later, checkpoint resumption is already enabled by default — you only need to opt in for alert routing. Maya also previewed what is coming in 4.8, including a dry-run mode that may catch up to 90% of transformation errors before they reach production.

The full recording and slides are available in your customer portal under Resources > Webinars. If you have questions, reply to this email or join our office hours on Thursday, June 12.

Thanks for being with us!

— The Product Team

cases.source:
Starting in version 2.4, our data platform caches query results in Redis instead of Memcached. This document explains why the change was made and what you should watch for.

The old Memcached layer stored serialized JSON with a maximum value size of 1 MB. Large analytic results simply bypassed the cache, so the heaviest queries hit the database every time. During the March incident, a report generator issued about 4,200 identical queries per minute, and the primary database cluster saturated.

The new Redis cache raises the limit to 512 MB and stores results using MessagePack, which cuts payload size roughly in half. Keys are namespaced by tenant, for example tenant:48291:report:monthly, and every entry carries a TTL of 900 seconds. Entries may be evicted early under memory pressure, since the cache runs in allkeys-lru mode.

Two behaviors differ from the old system. First, cache invalidation is now event-driven: when an ingestion job completes, it publishes a message on the internal topic invalidate.v1, and a worker purges the affected keys. Because delivery is asynchronous, a client may see stale data for up to a few seconds after a write. Second, failures are non-fatal. If Redis is unreachable, queries fall through to the database and log a warning; the cache is an optimization, not a dependency.

Nothing in the API changes. Callers still go through QueryService, and the Cache-Control-style flag no_cache=true still bypasses caching entirely.

When debugging, check the metrics dashboard first: cache_hits and cache_misses per minute will show whether traffic is reaching the cache at all. A hit rate below 40 percent usually means keys are being evicted too quickly, often due to memory pressure on the shared cluster. Do not treat a cold cache after a deploy as a bug; entries are not persisted across restarts by design, so the first minutes of traffic will always miss.

Engineering Update: Dashboard Redesign — Sprint 14 Recap

Team, here's where we stand on the dashboard redesign after this sprint.

Progress
The new layout shipped to staging on March 3 behind the `dash_v2` feature flag. The grid component now renders in under 90 ms for a typical 40-widget workspace, down from roughly 340 ms in v1, thanks to the virtualized renderer. We also migrated 28 of 31 widgets to the new API contract; the remaining three (audit log, cost explorer, and SLO heatmaps) need backend pagination support landing in Sprint 15.

What changed
- Dark mode is now computed from design tokens rather than hardcoded palettes, cutting CSS bundle size by 41 KB.
- The filter bar saves state to `/user/prefs` with a 250 ms debounce, so refreshes no longer wipe active filters.
- Empty states now show suggested queries instead of a blank canvas. Early usability sessions with five internal users were positive, though two found the suggestions noisy; we're adding a dismiss control.

Known issues
1. Chart tooltips clip at the right edge on viewports narrower than 1024 px. A fix is in review (PR #2317).
2. Real-time tiles reconnect with a full refetch after network drops instead of resuming from the last sequence number. Fix targeted for March 12.
3. The export job queue can back up if more than 50 exports are requested in a minute; the queue now sheds load gracefully, but we want proper backpressure before GA.

Metrics
Staging traffic shows a 12% drop in p95 time-to-interactive and an 18% reduction in JS payload after code splitting. Error rates are flat. Note these numbers come from a synthetic load rig, so they may shift under real traffic — treat them as directional until we've had two weeks of dogfooding.

Next steps
- Sprint 15: finish the last three widget migrations, land the tooltip fix, and add the backpressure mechanism.
- March 17: freeze visual changes and begin a two-week internal dogfood.
- GA target remains April 7, assuming dogfood metrics hold and no P1s are open.

If you own a widget or panel and haven't checked it under `dash_v2`, please do so this week — migration notes are in the #dash-redesign channel. Questions, edge cases, or complaints welcome; especially complaints, they're cheaper to fix now.

Thanks to everyone who crunched the renderer work — it was the riskiest piece and it landed clean.

- Dark mode is now driven by design tokens instead of hardcoded palettes, which shaved 41 KB off the CSS bundle.
- The filter bar saves state to `/user/prefs` with a 250 ms debounce, so refreshing the page no longer wipes out your active filters.
- Empty states now show suggested queries rather than a blank canvas. Early usability sessions with five internal users went well, though two found the suggestions a bit noisy — we're adding a dismiss control in response.

**Known issues**

1. Chart tooltips clip at the right edge on viewports narrower than 1024 px. A fix is in review (PR #2317).
2. Real-time tiles do a full refetch after network drops instead of resuming from the last sequence number. Fix is targeted for March 12.
3. The export job queue can back up if more than 50 exports come in within a minute. It now sheds load gracefully, but we want proper backpressure in place before GA.

**Metrics**

Staging traffic shows a 12% drop in p95 time-to-interactive and an 18% smaller JS payload after code splitting. Error rates are flat. One caveat: these numbers come from a synthetic load rig, so they may shift under real traffic — treat them as directional until we've had two weeks of dogfooding.

**Next steps**

- **Sprint 15:** finish the last three widget migrations, land the tooltip fix, and add the backpressure mechanism.
- **March 17:** freeze visual changes and kick off a two-week internal dogfood.
- **GA target:** still April 7, assuming dogfood metrics hold and no P1s are open.

If you own a widget or panel and haven't checked it under `dash_v2` yet, please do so this week — migration notes are in the #dash-redesign channel. Questions, edge cases, and complaints are all welcome — especially complaints, since they're cheaper to fix now.

Finally, a big thanks to everyone who worked on the renderer. It was the riskiest piece of this project, and it landed clean.

Engineering update: Security patch for the ingestion service (CVE-2044-339215)

Overview
We are shipping an emergency security patch, version 3.14.2, for the ingestion service (codename "Ferrofluid") to address CVE-2044-339215, a deserialization vulnerability in the payload-verification layer. The issue was found during an internal audit on March 11 and allows an authenticated user with read-only credentials to trigger remote code execution by submitting a malformed protobuf payload.

Impact
No customer data has been affected. Our logs show about 312 anomalous requests from a staging tenant, all traced to our own test harness. Production tenants were not exposed, because the vulnerable code path is only reachable when the legacy flag enable_legacy_deserializers is enabled, which is currently true on 2 of 41 shards.

The fix
The patch replaces the reflection-based deserializer with an explicit schema validator and rejects any payload exceeding 256 KB. Version 3.14.2 also adds stricter input sanitization and improves audit logging so future anomalies surface within minutes rather than days.

Rollout plan
1. Canary deployment to the staging cluster today at 17:00 UTC.
2. Rollout to shard groups A and B on Thursday, March 14, followed by the remaining shards on Friday.
3. Legacy deserializers will be disabled by default starting with version 3.15.0; teams may request a temporary extension through the platform channel.

Action items
- Team leads: confirm no service depends on oversized payloads before Thursday.
- On-call: watch for a spike in 422 responses during the canary window; a small increase is expected.
- Everyone: do not re-enable legacy flags in production without a security review.

Questions or concerns? Ping the #ferrofluid-security channel. Thanks to the platform team for the fast turnaround on the audit findings, and to everyone who helped validate the patch in staging.

— Platform Engineering
